significance.justification: A verified-true result would license the conclusion that "obligatory marking helps only when the marked dimension is task-relevant," a form-(iii) double-dissociation law relating grammatical obligation and task relevance to reasoning accuracy, together with a form-(ii) claim that marking causally preserves otherwise-dropped information. This would fix expectations for untested feature–task combinations and sharpen the interpretation of multilingual performance gaps documented by MGSM (Shi et al., ICLR 2023): the phenomenon is the selective accuracy interaction, while the proposed mechanism is a language-imposed attention or tracking scaffold rather than a language-wide proficiency effect. Verified false and verified true are determinate alternatives; a robust null would rule out obligatory grammar as a general scaffold in current LLMs, whereas a positive result would support that mechanism across several independently varying grammatical dimensions. In the topic-substitution check, the generic question of how language relates to AI intelligence would not itself earn this score—the claim's specific marking-by-relevance law and causal explanation supply the above-median constraint.

reach.justification: The transferable handle is the design rule embodied by "INSERT explicit marking (or STRIP it)": add explicit encoding of the dimension a task requires, rather than merely choosing a generally high-performing language. This is ex ante because prompt or interface designers can add evidential, number, definiteness, or gender marking before reasoning occurs, leaving an action window for prompting, auditing, or system design. After selecting or re-extracting the relevant grammatical feature in another model, the conclusion predicts a qualitative relation—benefit when that dimension is relevant and no general benefit otherwise—across the asserted four dimensions and multiple multilingual model families, although it does not predict transferable effect sizes. The topic-substitution check retains the high score because the broad language–intelligence topic alone supplies neither this task-conditional design rule nor its usable prediction for researchers and practitioners who build or deploy multilingual reasoning systems.
